rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad refers readers to his notes on 87:2 and 91:7 for his rendering of sawwa; the following sentence breaks off after mentioning God's creating.
rows.anchor: For this rendering of sawwa, see note 1 on 87:2 and note 5 on 91:7. The stress on God's creating

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links the instruction to patience under God's judgment with the preceding promises: the righteous meet bliss and evildoers suffering in the hereafter.
rows.anchor: This connects with the preceding mention of the life to come, in which the righteous will meet with bliss, and the evildoers with suffering.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses the night devotion as extending to every time one is awake.
rows.anchor: I.e., at all times of wakefulness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad presents the night devotion as consolation whenever unhappiness presses in and one's surroundings seem dark.
rows.anchor: I.e., "whenever unhappiness oppresses thee and all seems dark around thee".

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says the sūra takes its name from al-mursalat in its opening verse, which refers to the Qur'an's gradual revelation.
rows.anchor: al-mursalat which appears in the first verse (and which obviously refers to the gradual revelation of the Qur'an)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad places the sūra between al-Humazah (104) and Qaf (50), almost certainly in the Prophet's fourth mission year.
rows.anchor: between surahs 104 (Al-Humazah) and 50 (Qaf), i.e., almost certainly in the fourth year of the Prophet's mission

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says that without full awareness of God, a person cannot distinguish what is morally right from wrong.
rows.anchor: so long as man is not fully aware of the existence of God, he cannot really discern between what is morally right or wrong

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God is just, Asad says He does not punish people before they attain moral discernment, linking this principle to 6:31.
rows.anchor: since God is just, He does not punish anyone who has not yet attained to such a discernment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad clarifies that al-ula literally means the first life, here rendered as this world.
rows.anchor: Lit., "in the first [life]"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad points to 7:137's account of Pharaoh's destruction and its corresponding note as a parallel for the worldly punishment.
rows.anchor: last sentence of 7:137 - "We utterly destroyed all that Pharaoh and his people had wrought, and all that they had built"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad cites well-authenticated traditions: while the Prophet sought to persuade leading pagan Meccan chiefs and the wider community, blind follower Abd Allah ibn Shurayh (Ibn Umm Maktum) asked him to repeat or explain earlier Qur'anic passages.
rows.anchor: as recorded in many well-authenticated Traditions, the Prophet was engrossed in a conversation with some of the most influential chieftains of pagan Mecca

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says Muhammad was annoyed by the interruption, turned away from the blind man, and was immediately reproved in the sūra's first ten verses.
rows.anchor: Annoyed by this interruption of what he momentarily regarded as a more important endeavour, Muhammad "frowned and turned away" from the blind man

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reports that in later years the Prophet welcomed Ibn Umm Maktum with a humble acknowledgment that God had rebuked him on his account.
rows.anchor: In later years he often greeted Ibn Umm Maktum with these words of humility

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad argues that conduct amounting to minor discourtesy in an ordinary person became a major sin deserving divine rebuke when committed by a prophet.
rows.anchor: what would have been a minor act of discourtesy on the part of an ordinary human being, assumed the aspect of a major sin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says the use of third-person forms in verses 1–2 particularly sharpens the Qur'anic rebuke.
rows.anchor: the sharp Qur'anic rebuke (stressed, in particular, by the use of the third-person form in verses 1-2)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad takes the Prophet's public conveyance of God's reproof as evidence that revelation is objective, connecting it to 53:3.
rows.anchor: in conveying God's reproof of him to the world at large, the Prophet "does not speak out of his own desire" (cf. 53:3)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The self-sufficient person is, in Asad's reading, someone who feels no need for divine guidance, especially the arrogant pagan chiefs addressed by the Prophet.
rows.anchor: who does not feel the need of divine guidance: a reference to the arrogant pagan chieftains

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads qutila here as man's self-destruction and points readers to his note 9 on sūra 74 for this rendering.
rows.anchor: For my rendering of qutila as "he destroys himself", see surah 74, note 9.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad explains that human nature is determined for the organic roles of body and mind and for adapting to natural conditions.
rows.anchor: organic functions which man's body and mind are to fulfil, and the natural conditions

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although verses 18–22 use the past tense, Asad says they describe a recurring phenomenon.
rows.anchor: Verses 18-22, although formulated in the past tense, obviously describe a recurrent phenomenon.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad reads the question as warning that no one is wholly immune to fitnah; he compares 8:25 and says the answer comes in 82:9.
rows.anchor: no human being is ever entirely immune against "that temptation to evil (fitnah)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says God endowed each person with qualities and abilities suited to that individual's life and environment.
rows.anchor: endowed thee with all the qualities and abilities relevant to the exigencies of thy individual life and thy environment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad explains human proportion as including bodily needs and emotional urges alongside intellectual and spiritual perceptions.
rows.anchor: a being subject to physical needs and emotional urges, and at the same time endowed with intellectual and spiritual perceptions

words: فِىٓ أَىِّ صُورَةٍۢ مَّا شَآءَ رَكَّبَكَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because both sides of human nature are willed by God, Asad says there is no inherent moral conflict between flesh and spirit.
rows.anchor: both these aspects of the human condition are - as stressed in the next verse - God-willed and, therefore, morally justified.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad connects the spring drunk by those near to God with the drinks described in 76:5–6.
rows.anchor: Cf. 76:5-6 and the corresponding notes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad says earthly life is painful toil for everyone, whether consciously recognized or not, because sorrow, pain, drudgery, and worry outweigh rare happiness; this toil leads to meeting God at resurrection.
rows.anchor: sorrow, pain, drudgery and worry by far outweigh the rare moments of true happiness and satisfaction

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad glosses "his people" as those who share the same sinful inclinations, with a comparison to note 14 on 75:33.
rows.anchor: people of the same sinful inclinations

words: وَإِذَا قُرِئَ عَلَيْهِمُ ٱلْقُرْءَانُ لَا يَسْجُدُونَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad explains the Qur'an's call to prostration by its consistent stress on God's law of unceasing change and progression throughout existence.
rows.anchor: seeing how consistently it stresses the divine law of unceasing change and progression in all that exists

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūra takes its title from at-tariq, which Asad renders as that which comes in the night.
rows.anchor: At-Tariq (That Which Comes In The Night)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad dates the sūra relatively early, probably to the Prophet's fourth mission year.
rows.anchor: in the fourth year of the Prophet's

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad expands the call to consider the returning sky and splitting earth as a way to grasp God's creative and re-creative power more fully.
rows.anchor: And, finally, in order to grasp more fully God's power of creation and re-creation, consider
